demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
Case Vignette: Marcos R.

Marcos R. is a 22-year-old HVAC technician, single, who presents for an initial evaluation at the urging of his older sister. He is a soft-spoken man with a guarded posture, his eyes often fixed on a point just past my shoulder. He has been unable to work for the past three weeks.

The event that changed everything happened four months ago. Marcos had been on the job for only eight months, working for a small residential heating and cooling company. He was proud of his work, of being able to fix things with his hands, of the independence the job gave him. On a Tuesday afternoon in late August, he was called to replace a faulty compressor in the attic of a two-story home. The homeowner, a man in his late fifties named Mr. Delgado, was friendly, even brought him a glass of water. Marcos remembers the heat in the attic was suffocating, the air thick with dust and fiberglass. He was rushing, trying to finish before the worst of the afternoon sun. He disassembled the old unit, but when he lifted the heavy compressor, his grip slipped on the sweat-slicked metal. It crashed down through the attic floor, straight through the ceiling of the living room below.

Marcos can still hear the sound. Not just the crash, but the wet, sickening thud that followed, and then Mr. Delgado’s wife screaming. He scrambled down the pull-down ladder, his heart hammering. Mr. Delgado was on the floor, a jagged piece of ceiling drywall and the compressor pinning his leg. There was blood on the beige carpet. Marcos called 911. He remembers his own hands shaking so badly he could barely press the numbers. He remembers the paramedics pushing him aside. Mr. Delgado’s leg was crushed. He required multiple surgeries and a long rehabilitation. He will walk with a permanent limp.

In the weeks that followed, Marcos tried to go back to work. He told himself it was an accident, that it could have happened to anyone. But his hands would start to tremble the moment he picked up a tool. He would break into a cold sweat when a customer asked him to go into an attic. He began to see Mr. Delgado’s face, the look of shock and pain, in his mind’s eye whenever he closed his eyes. The sound of the crash replays in his head, triggered by the clatter of a dropped pan in his own kitchen or the slam of a car door.

He has stopped working entirely. He spends most of his days in his small apartment, the blinds drawn. He has a persistent, gnawing feeling that he is a bad person, that he is dangerous. He avoids his coworkers, who have called to check on him. He cannot bring himself to call Mr. Delgado’s family to apologize, though he has drafted a dozen letters in his head. He feels a constant, low-grade shame that sits in his chest like a stone. He has started drinking a few beers every evening to quiet his mind enough to sleep, but he still wakes up drenched in sweat, having dreamed of the fall, of the sound, of the blood.

He describes feeling “hollow” and “cut off” from everyone he used to know. He no longer goes to his weekly soccer games with his friends. He cancelled a date with a woman he had been seeing casually. He feels like a different person now—a person who breaks things, who hurts people. He is terrified of his own potential for destruction. He says he feels like he is living in a fog, waiting for the other shoe to drop. He is here because his sister found him sitting in the dark at 3 p.m. and refused to leave until he agreed to talk to someone.
